item.title: Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty
item.description:
Raids on Overijssel livestock businesses over fraud and cruelty

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Investigators from the food and product safety board NVWA have raided the homes and businesses of two livestock traders in Overijssel over suspected fraud and transporting sick animals.

The raids took place on September 30, the NVWA said on Wednesday. Investigators seized business records, phones, used ear tags and a pair of pliers for removing ear tags.

Every cow in the Netherlands must be registered and carry an ear tag with a unique number, so animals can be traced quickly if there is a disease outbreak or meat turns out to be contaminated.

Unregistered animals
At one trader’s premises, 88 animals were registered at a different address or not registered at all. At the other, 19 animals were incorrectly registered. Cattle without the mandatory ear tags were found at both sites.

With help from the police, investigators also stopped a lorry that had left one of the traders’ premises early in the morning. None of the 21 cattle on board were registered to his address. Another 32 cattle belonging to the same trader were found on a farm elsewhere in Overijssel. They had been imported but never registered in the Netherlands.

One trader’s business was registered on paper at the other’s address, keeping it out of sight. Cattle from the Netherlands and abroad were being kept there. Animals may only be gathered for sale or slaughter at approved collection centres, which have strict rules on cleaning and disinfecting livestock trucks to stop disease from spreading.

Sick cows
Inspectors also found a shed of cows in poor condition. Some could no longer stand and others had severe inflammation. One of the traders is suspected of transporting the animals even though they were too sick to be moved. The NVWA believes he then kept them because he could no longer sell them or have them slaughtered.

A vet put three cows down on the spot. The NVWA has taken administrative measures to make sure the rest get the care they need.

Neither trader has been arrested. The criminal investigation is being led by the public prosecution department’s specialist unit for environmental and fraud cases (Functioneel Parket). The NVWA told broadcaster NOS it could not say how it came across the pair.

item.title: MPs back age verification plan for online adult services ads
item.description:
MPs back age verification plan for online adult services ads

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch MPs have backed a plan to introduce compulsory age verification for websites advertising sexual services, to protect children from exploitation.

An amendment tabled by opposition parties JA21 and ChristenUnie would require website operators to check the identity and age of anyone whose image is used in an advert, by comparing photo ID with a photo taken when the order is placed.

The vote went against the advice of justice minister David van Weel, who said he “did not disagree” with the principle of the amendment but questioned if it was the most suitable way to change the law.

Van Weel advised MPs to wait until the cabinet produced its own plan after consulting the Council of State and checking whether the amendment complied with European law.

“The amendment is the fastest way to change the law, but sometimes you end up cutting corners,” he said. The Senate still has to vote on the law.

The child protection organisation CKM said it was pleased the amendment had been passed, after earlier attempts to solve the problem through a voluntary agreement failed.

Voluntary approach failed

An investigation by CKM found that 80% of minors in cases of exploitation and abuse were advertised on legitimate websites.

Major adult services sites signed a covenant eight years ago with the police and prosecution service in which they pledged to alert the authorities to signs of abuse.

The agreement followed the conclusion of a notorious abuse case in Valkenburg, Limburg, in which a 16-year-old girl was forced to have sex with 29 men in a hotel room after another man had posted her details online.

Shamir Ceuleers, head of the CKM, told Nieuwsuur: “These are basically victims of human trafficking. They might not be advertised as underage, but there are enough signs in these adverts that something isn’t right.”

He pointed out that MPs had been trying for five years to make websites legally liable for checking the contents of adverts before they were put online because it was clear self-regulation was ineffective.

“Parliament has been asking for regulation by law since 2021, and with good reason,” he said. “The Valkenburg case is brought up every time, but even today there are underage children [advertised] online and that is unacceptable.”

item.title: Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule
item.description:
Judge signals support for Booking’s two-day office rule

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An Amsterdam judge has signalled she is likely to back Booking.com in its attempt to make staff work at least two days a week in the office, the Financieele Dagblad has reported.

The travel platform faced off against its works council (an elected employee body whose consent is needed to change working conditions) over whether it is reasonable to require in-office presence at that rate for all its workers.

“Two days is really very little, I’m just telling it like it is,” the judge said during Tuesday’s hearing. For over three years, Booking has held the two-day-a-week rule as a recommendation, but now wants it enforced as a mandatory measure.

The headquarters, on Amsterdam’s Oosterdok, cover more than 65,000 square metres. Booking agreed in 2016 to pay €270 million for the building and its land-use rights, according to filings by its parent company with US regulators. The average attendance rate by staff is 27%, according to the FD.

Dozens of employees sat in on the hearing. The company told the court that making office attendance mandatory was a “small step”, and argued that working only from home can harm staff’s mental health.

The works council disagreed, and one employee told the court he commutes an hour to the office, only to sit on Zoom meetings all day with colleagues in other countries.

The council also spoke about mental wellbeing and said that making office days compulsory could harm staff by taking away their autonomy. A lawyer for the council also noted that Booking is economically thriving regardless of low office attendance.

But the judge seemed to lean towards the arguments of the business. “You might think Dutch judges are strange, but we find working 40% of the time in the office perfectly normal,” she told the courtroom, where the audience was partly international.

The two sides have been given a week to reach an agreement. If they fail, the court will rule at the end of October.

item.title: Unions and cabinet start budget talks on social security reform
item.description:
Unions and cabinet start budget talks on social security reform

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Unions and employers say they have had constructive talks with ministers as they try to end the impasse over next year’s budget.

Prime minister Rob Jetten said the “real negotiations still have to start”, but initial discussions had been good-natured and positive.

The government needs to plug a gap of around €6 billion in the public finances after it agreed to abandon plans to reduce the welfare bill by cutting the long-term incapacity benefit WIA and shorten the maximum term for unemployment pay (WW).

The three largest trade unions, FNV, CNV and VCP, last week called off a series of planned strikes that were called to press the government to save the social security “safety net”.

FNV chairman Hans Spekman said the unions were prepared to look at ways to make the benefits system more cost effective and save money, but the cabinet had not set a target figure. “We are not being asked to meet an objective,” he said.

The minority government hopes to secure support from the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt in order to get the votes it needs to pass its budget through both houses of parliament.

Capital gains tax

But finance minister Eelco Heinen also wants to make concessions to right-wing parties on issues such as the reform of the “box 3” income tax mechanism, so that it taxes capital gains rather than asset values.

Heinen has already had to revise his original plans after right-wing parties were critical of his proposal to bring around 850,000 small investors and savers below the threshold for wealth taxes in order to make up the budget shortfall.

There was another setback for the cabinet in the senate, where the farmers’ party BBB stepped up its demands for the government to go back to the drawing board on nitrogen pollution.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen unveiled a package of measures before the summer recess to bring down nitrogen compound emissions and protect Natura-2000 conservation areas, including a voluntary buyout scheme.

He warned that there was little room to water down the measures if the government wants to lift the “nitrogen blockade” that has held up construction projects, while the left-wing party Pro has warned it will not accept any weakening of the plans.

BBB block threat

But the BBB says the plans are unacceptable to farms and rural businesses and have warned they will block the budget in the upper house, where they are the second largest party, unless Van Essen withdraws them.

Jetten said during a debate in the Senate that there was little room to renegotiate the package. “It is ultimately up to the BBB in both houses to decide if they want to be work with us on realising the nitrogen measures and whether they want to keep tying it in with the tax plans,” he said.

BBB senator Henk Marquat Scholz told Nieuwsuur his party was “keen to go along with the cabinet, as long as the nitrogen letter is taken off the table.”

item.title: NSC loses last seat in parliament as MEP Dirk Gotink quits party
item.description:
NSC loses last seat in parliament as MEP Dirk Gotink quits party

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The last elected politician representing Nieuw Sociaal Contract (NSC), the party formed three years ago by former CDA MP Pieter Omtzigt, has resigned in a row over whether to work with a new hardline Eurosceptic group.

Dirk Gotink, NSC’s only member in the European Parliament, quit the party over the decision to explore a possible collaboration with Mona Keijzer’s Project 2029, a right-wing conservative movement that sees the European Union as a federal superstate in the making.

Gotink, 45, said in a post on LinkedIn that seeking closer ties with Keijzer, another former Christian Democrat (CDA) MP, was “incomprehensible”.

“When it comes to Europe, we take a very different stance,” he said. “For me the EU is a precondition for our freedom and prosperity … Sowing doubt about the importance of the EU is not just irresponsible but also goes against the interests of the Netherlands.”

The party’s board said it had invited Keijzer to be a guest speaker at this weekend’s conference in Breda without any promise of entering into a formal partnership. But Gotink said the appearance of the former farmers’ party (BBB) housing minister was a “clear choice of political direction”.

NSC leaderless

Gotink has been the only NSC member in any parliament since the general election last October, when the party lost all 20 seats in the Dutch parliament that it won two years earlier, three months after its foundation. It has had no leader since Omtzigt’s successor, Eddy van Hijum, quit in January.

Gotink said he was grateful for the opportunity given him by Omtzigt, but he would be continuing as an independent MEP within the conservative EPP group.

“He redefined Christian Democrat thinking and tied it to tangible ideas such as basic living standards and the rule of law,” he told AD.nl. “He gave me the chance to contribute as an MEP. I am very grateful to him for that.”

Omtzigt founded NSC in August 2023 with a promise to make government in the Netherlands more accountable through constitutional reform and improve people’s basic standard of living (bestaanszekerheid).

Coalition with PVV

But after the party entered a coalition with the far-right PVV, the right-wing liberal VVD and the farmers’ party BBB, NSC fell apart under pressure from PVV leader Geert Wilders, who accused it of obstructing his asylum policies.

Omtzigt resigned as party leader and stepped down as an MP last year on health grounds, having taken several months off work with burnout symptoms. In a parting press conference he said the “poisonous” political climate in the Netherlands was preventing politicians from tackling the country’s real problems.

Omtzigt had quit the CDA in 2021 following a dispute with the party leadership, which wanted the campaigning backbench MP to be offered a “position elsewhere”.

His efforts to seek justice for families who were wrongly accused of benefit fraud in what became known as the toeslagenaffaire triggered the downfall of Mark Rutte’s third coalition government, which included the CDA, in 2021.

He stood for the leadership of the CDA in 2020 but lost narrowly to Hugo de Jonge, the health minister during the coronavirus pandemic. The third-placed candidate in that race was Mona Keijzer.

item.title: Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims
item.description:
Dutch government told to rule on 140,000 Ukrainian asylum claims

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The European Court of Justice has ordered the Dutch government to process the asylum applications of 140,000 Ukrainian refugees, adding to the pressure on an overstretched system.

Ukrainians who fled the country in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022 are covered by the European Union’s temporary protection rules, which give them the right to live, work and receive medical care in the Netherlands.

Under Dutch rules they are also required to apply for asylum, but until now the immigration service IND has shelved their applications because the European regulations give them more rights.

The European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Luxembourg said in a judgment last week that the rules requiring the Netherlands to process all asylum claims within 21 months also applied to people who fled Ukraine.

The case was brought by a man from the Chinese Uighur minority who was married to a Ukrainian woman and lived in Ukraine with his wife and child before the invasion.

He won a ruling at the district court in The Hague forcing the asylum minister to rule on his claim by January 2024. The court also imposed a conditional penalty on the government of €100 foe every day that a decision is overdue, up to a maximum of €7,500.

Extra pressure

The government appealed, and the case was referred to the ECJ, which said the man had the right to claim asylum as a third country national through the regular procedure even though he was already protected by the EU rules for Ukrainians.

Asylum minister Bart van den Brink admitted that the decision would put “extra pressure” on the system, but the court also recognised that the Netherlands needed time to process all 140,000 claims.

“For a long time we chose not to process claims from Ukrainians because of the fact that they were already protected,” he told NOS. “It’s also because it was a very large number. Now the court has clearly said we have to do it.”

The Netherlands is one of the few countries in the EU that require Ukrainian refugees to apply for asylum through the regular channels in addition to the EU’s temporary protection rules, which are currently valid until March 2028 but are reviewed every year.

“In hindsight it wasn’t such a good idea to link temporary protection to the submission of a claim for asylum,” asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom said.

Waiting list

Vluchtelingenwerk, the Dutch refugee council, said the need to have asylum claims processed would cause “more worry and uncertainty” for Ukrainians.

“Returning to Ukraine is not a realistic option at the moment, given that there is no sign of the war ending.” a spokesman told Dutch News.

“Vluchtelingenwerk hopes there will be a clear and above all sustainable plan for Ukrainians in the Netherlands, so that these people, who have already been through so much, know where they stand.”

Van den Brink said the government planned to deal with the Ukrainian applications in reverse order, beginning with people who have just arrived in the Netherlands and then working through the 5,000 who are currently on the waiting list for a first response from the government.

Ricky van Oers, lecturer in migration law at Radboud University in Nijmegen, said European rules allowed the government to take more time to process applications when there was a large number from a single country at once.

“They can also decide to prioritise certain groups, such as families,” he said.

item.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy
item.description:
The Song of Stork and Dromedary: Nobel worthy

October 7, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Novelist Anjet Daanje has been tipped as a serious contender for the Nobel prize in literature and, from her 2022 work The Song of Stork and Dromedary, for very good reason.

Published in Dutch as Het lied van ooievaar en dromedaris, the book is loosely based on the life of Emily Brontë, the author of Wuthering Heights. The work opens in 1847, with a villager laying out the body of Eliza May Drayden, who, like Brontë, has written a book widely derided at the time it was published but would go on to become a classic.

The opening scene is tinged with the Gothic horror of Wuthering Heights, Drayden’s eyes refuse to close for her burial.

The next 650 pages follow 11 interconnect stories that orbit around Drayden, and her sister Millicent, the fictionalised Charlotte Brontë who authored of Jane Eyre. Similar again to Wuthering Heights, all are largely set on the moors in England, though the final story takes the reader to the Daanje’s hometown of Groningen.

Rather than a traditional narrative, the book is written like an expansive biography, incorporating news articles, excerpts from diaries, letters, citations from fictional biographies and even parts of Drayden’s novel.

Each of the tales could be novellas in their own right, vivid and sometimes nail-biting, sending the reader off on tangents such as the mistreatment of two half-German sisters during the Second World War, or a pair of French half-sisters whose shared father creates a wedge between them.

The nature of sisterhood and the relationship between various female characters is one of the central themes of The Song of Stork and Dromedary. The work also reflects on the status of women at different times across the novel’s 200-year span.

Death is another important theme. Drayden’s death, with which the book opens, is an event that brings characters together but also tears them apart.

Anjet Daanje published eight novels before The Remembered Soldier (De herinnerde soldaat) became a hit in 2019. It was longlisted for the Libris Literature Prize, took home the F. Bordewijk Prize and the English-translation, which was published in 2025, was longlisted for International Booker Prize and included on The New York Times Book Review’s 100 Notable Books of 2025.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary took home both the Boekenbon Literature Prize and the Libris Literature Prize, the first book to ever net both awards. It was named the Best Book of the Century by the NRC newspaper. The English translation was published this year.

In 2023, Daanje was awarded the Constantijn Huygens Prize for her oeuvre.

The book was translated by David McKay, who also translated War and Turpentine by Stefan Hertmans and Multatuli’s Max Havelaar. He renders the complicated work thoughtfully, retaining Daanje’s character.

The Song of Stork and Dromedary is compelling and brilliant, and the author is worthy of the highest honour in literature.

The Nobel prize for literature winner will be announced on Thursday by the 18 members of the Swedish Academy.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

item.title: Cancer diagnoses set to rise by almost a quarter by 2045
item.description:
Cancer diagnoses set to rise by almost a quarter by 2045

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of new cancer diagnoses in the Netherlands is expected to rise by almost a quarter to nearly 170,000 a year by 2045, mainly because the population is growing and ageing, the national cancer centre IKNL said on Wednesday.

The number of people dying of cancer each year is also set to rise, from just over 46,000 in 2024 to just over 57,000. Some 136,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

IKNL said in its new 20-year projections that the age-adjusted risk of getting cancer will stay mostly the same, while the risk of dying from the disease will continue falling.

The increase is driven by the growing number of older people. Five-year survival rates have improved for decades, reaching 72% for women and 69% for men, up from 55% and 42% in the early 1990s.

Skin cancer is set to become the most common form of cancer among both men and women, overtaking breast and prostate cancer. Besides ageing, the rise is mainly down to sun exposure and sunburn earlier in life, IKNL researcher Jaike Schilte-Praagman told NU.nl. People are also getting suspicious spots checked sooner, she said.

The projections do not account for new treatments, and there may be breakthroughs in the coming years. “We don’t know what treatments are still to come, so we can’t include them in our calculations,” Schilte-Praagman added.

“Without targeted measures, demand for cancer care threatens to grow faster than capacity,” IKNL board chair Ernst Kuipers told the website.

At least a third of all cancer diagnoses could be prevented through healthier lifestyles and living environments, according to cancer charity KWF.

IKNL calculated in 2024 that if no young people smoked by 2032 and the adult smoking rate fell to 5%, some 120,000 cases of lung, bladder and oesophageal cancer would be avoided by 2045.

“You can’t just tell people to live more healthily,” Schilte-Praagman said. “The government has a role to play too. It has to create an environment that makes healthy choices easier.”

item.title: MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises
item.description:
MPs want 130,000 trained civilians ready for national crises

October 7, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

MPs want 130,000 civilians trained to support the police, army and emergency services during major crises, and have asked the cabinet to open up defence ministry facilities to help make it happen.

A majority in parliament backed a motion by the centrist Christian Democrat CDA on Tuesday calling for that number of so-called civilian reservists within 4 years, public broadcaster NOS reported.

The volunteers would not join the armed forces, but would be a support force around them. Their specific role would be to stop chaos breaking out in the first three days of a disaster, when the emergency and security services are not expected to cope alone.

According to NOS, they would be trained in 3 areas – technical, logistics and security – drawing on people such as mechanics, drivers and security guards.
MPs want the cabinet to help in kind rather than with money, by making defence ministry training grounds and classrooms available free of charge. The cabinet has said it shares the aim.

From 1,000 to 130,000
The 130,000 figure matches the long-term target of De BurgerReserve, a privately run organisation that began training volunteers last year. Its two-day course at the national training centre in Vught ends with a simulated disaster and is paid for by employers and private individuals.

The organisation has trained around 1,000 people so far this year, NOS said. Reaching 130,000 within 4 years would mean training more than 30,000 people a year, while the courses listed on its website take up to 64 people each.

Fears over cyberattacks and strikes on infrastructure through AI have spread rapidly this year, with intelligence service AIVD warning the Netherlands has not been at such a high level of risk since the second world war.

Catching up
The vote follows a government campaign urging households to prepare for the first 72 hours of a crisis. Every home received an emergency booklet over the winter, and in February half of households said they now stock emergency provisions accordingly.

Karen van Oudenhoven-van der Zee, director of the social and cultural planning bureau SCP, told current affairs programme Nieuwsuur that investment in the armed forces was out of proportion to the attention paid to people and society.

She said the 2027 budget sets aside €40 million for neighbourhoods and communities, falling to €20 million in the two years after that.

“When it comes to resilience, we have catching up to do,” she said.

item.title: Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe
item.description:
Shepherds turn to dogs to defend sheep from wolves on the Veluwe

October 6, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Shepherds in the Veluwe region have come up with a novel solution to deter wolf attacks by hiring Italian mountain dogs to guard their sheep.

Stichting Schapedrift Ermelo, a volunteer organisation that tends a herd of sheep on the heathlands in Gelderland, acquired two Maremmano-Abruzzese sheepdogs this summer to protect the herd from prowling wolves.

The forested Veluwe region has the biggest concentration of wolves in the Netherlands, with seven packs living in an area of 1,000 square kilometres, since the predators returned in 2019.

The organisation has put up eight-foot electrocuted fences around its sheep enclosure to keep wolves out, but the animals are still vulnerable when they are being herded across the heath.

“We see an increasing threat from wolves,” shepherd Marion Derks told Omroep Gelderland. “And there are a few walking round here that were interested in the sheep.”

The two white-haired dogs have been used for centuries to defend sheep. They are valued for their non-aggressive nature and alertness, Derks said.

“As soon as they see danger, you see their attitude change and they go into defensive mode,” she explained. “They make themselves bigger and more imposing and start barking.”

She said the dogs were not expected to confront or attack wolves. “Their presence is meant to stop the wolves approaching,” Derks explained. “Wolves will take easy prey but if they think it’s going to be too difficult, they’ll look for something else.”
